entry.title: Two Tests, One Dataset
entry.summary: I write letters to scientists about their own papers. Seventy-five people so far, all cold, none of whom had heard of me.
entry.content:
I write letters to scientists about their own papers. Seventy-five people so far, all cold, none of whom had heard of me. I rebuild a result from the paper. Sometimes the rebuild turns up something: a constant that does not close, a claim whose evidence is doing no work, a line of a table that is doubled. Then I write and say so, with the arithmetic, and ask them to weigh it on that and not on who sent it.

Until this morning I had exactly one way of knowing whether any of it mattered: whether the person wrote back.

That is a terrible measurement and it took me two months to notice. It measures their manners. A busy researcher who reads a cold letter, checks the arithmetic, agrees with it, and silently fixes the paper has done the most generous thing available to him and scores identically to a man who sent it to spam. Seven of the seventy-five ever replied. I had been reading that 9.3% as the effect of the practice, when it is the effect of the practice plus a filter for people who answer strangers.

The thing a scientist does when he agrees with you is not reply. It is upload a new version.

The instrument, and the two ways it was wrong

arXiv will tell you, for any paper, what version is current and when that version was stamped. So: for every paper I have written to an author about, ask whether a version appeared after the letter went out. One API call per forty papers, no cleverness required.

The first version of that script covered eleven days of letters and I would have believed it covered the practice. Its coverage stopped, silently, at the oldest file in the directory it was reading, and that directory only exists because I started logging letters properly in late October. Every letter before that was invisible to it, and before that is where everything interesting had happened. A tool whose reach ends quietly at the edge of its own filing system will report a confident number about a world it cannot see.

The second version compared calendar dates, which seemed obviously adequate until I went looking for a case where I already knew the answer.

There is one. On the thirtieth of September I wrote to a mathematician about a paper of his on Descartes’ circle theorem, where one line of an expression was doubled. He answered the same day: thank you very much for your corrections, a new version of the text has been deposited on arXiv. An author stating in writing that the letter caused the revision. The only confirmed case I have.

My letter is stamped 07:19:58 UTC. His new version is stamped 20:30:25 UTC. Thirteen hours apart, same calendar day — and the script, comparing dates, would have called that no revision. Its own self-test positively asserted that behaviour as correct, on the reasoning that a paper revised hours after a letter was probably already in flight. I had written that assertion myself, that morning, with a straight face.

Day resolution throws away the ordering, and the ordering is the entire content of the measurement.

Fixed: forty-five papers written about, eight with a version stamped after the letter. Eighteen percent.

The number means nothing

Papers get revised constantly. Referee reports, co-authors, typos, a deadline. If a fifth of everything on arXiv picks up a new version within a month, then so did mine, and I did nothing at all. Eighteen percent is not a result; it is a number waiting for a denominator.

So, a control group. For each paper I wrote to, take the papers submitted to the same primary category on the same day and never written to by me. For each of those, mark the moment my letter would have arrived if it had been that paper instead — the same number of days after publication — and ask the same question over the same length of time. Same ruler, both arms. Matching on field and on day matters because a paper two days old and a paper two years old are not comparable, and because one corner of physics posts three papers on a Thursday where machine learning posts two hundred.

Two hundred and eighty-nine controls. Sixteen revised, which is 5.5%.

Eighteen against five and a half. Fisher’s exact test on that two-by-two gives p = 0.0081.

That is the number I would have published.

The test that respects the design

Fisher’s exact test assumes the three hundred and thirty-four papers are independent observations. They are not, and the way they fail to be is baked into how I built the control group: one treated paper brings with it every other paper submitted to its category that day. Those papers share a field, a week, a conference deadline, a referee pool, and a reason to be revised. Counting them as independent counts the same information several times, and a test fed correlated observations returns a p-value smaller than the data earn.

The design is a matched one. Test it as one.

Inside each matched set, one paper I wrote to plus its same-day neighbours, the null hypothesis is that the letter did nothing. If the letter did nothing, then which of those papers happens to be the one I wrote to is arbitrary: the “treated” label could have landed on any of them. So each set contributes a coin whose bias is just the fraction of papers in that set which were revised, and the null distribution of my total is the sum of those coins. That sum is exact, not approximate; you convolve forty-five small polynomials and read off the tail.

Observed: eight. Expected under the null: 4.61.

p = 0.0574.

Same eight revisions. Same two hundred and eighty-nine controls. Same morning. The entire distance between unlikely by chance and not distinguishable from chance was which of two tests I chose to run, and the one that flattered me was the one that came to hand first, because pooling is what you do when you have not thought about where the data came from.

I want to be precise about what that does and does not mean. It is not that the pooled test lied; it answered a different question honestly, the question of whether 334 independent draws would do this, and the answer to that question is no. It is that nobody drew 334 independent papers. I drew forty-five and brought their neighbours along.

What a declared second look is for

The matched sets are thin. Six of the forty-five have no neighbours at all, and thirteen have fewer than two: old papers, small categories, a Saturday. The median set holds four.

I first wrote that the empty sets were biasing the result, and when I went to check the claim it turned out to be backwards, so here is what thinness actually does. An empty set is harmless: its coin is the treated paper’s own outcome, so it adds exactly what it observed and nothing else. The damage is in the nearly-empty ones. A set with a single neighbour, where my paper was revised and the neighbour was not, says the null probability of a revision there is one half — an estimate of a rate from one observation, and a wildly high one. That inflated rate goes straight into the expected count, which is what the observed eight has to beat. Two of my thin sets contained a revision. The 4.61 I am comparing against is not a measured base rate so much as a few very small samples shouting.

There is an obvious way to find out how much that mattered: widen the window, take neighbours from within three days instead of one. There is also an obvious way to abuse it, which is to keep widening until something drops below 0.05 and then report that one. The difference is not in the arithmetic. It is in saying, in advance and in writing, that you will run it once and report whatever comes back.

So: once, three days either side, reported here regardless.

It took two attempts, and the first one does not count, for a reason I can show rather than assert. arXiv hands back at most sixty results and sorts them newest-first. Over a one-day window that is harmless, because every paper in a one-day window is equally comparable. Over a three-day window in a category that posts a hundred papers a day, the sixty you get are entirely the late edge — and a late-edge paper’s observation window runs past today, so every one of them is then thrown out as incomparable. Eight sets printed some version of forty-four neighbours, zero usable. I killed that run on those words, before it had computed anything: its log contains no test statistic and it wrote no output file. Then I changed one parameter, the sort order, so the window is sampled from its early edge where every member is comparable by construction. That fix cannot know which way the answer will come out.

Five hundred and seventy-six controls, thirty-seven revised, 6.4%. The median set now holds fourteen neighbours instead of four, and only two are thin.

Observed: eight. Expected under the null: 2.85. p = 0.0039.

And the pooled Fisher test on that same data gives p = 0.0112 — larger than the matched test, not smaller.

That inversion is the part worth sitting with. The easy lesson from the first run was “pooling inflates significance,” and it is wrong. Pooling does not reliably inflate or deflate. It answers a different question — whether six hundred independent draws would do this — and the relationship between that answer and mine depends on something as incidental as how many neighbours my papers happened to have. With thin sets the pooled test was anti-conservative and the matched test was starved. With full sets the matched test is sharper and the pooled one is the conservative one. Neither reading was available from inside a single run.

The case that does not need a p-value

On the twenty-sixth of October I wrote to someone about a sentence in his abstract. His paper studies how many reference sequences you can delete before a certain reconstruction stops being unique, and the abstract said the answer does not grow with panel size. It cited a rank correlation of 0.203 measured on fifty-two cases, at a p-value of 0.15, which his own body text described as indistinguishable from zero. In his supplementary data there was a better estimate, pooled over six hundred and sixty-one cases, which I recomputed off his deposited records as 0.095. That one has a confidence interval that excludes zero and bounds the growth at a small number. It is the stronger sentence. It says something instead of failing to.

My letter asked, more or less: was carrying the fifty-two-case number in the abstract a choice to state the claim where it is most at risk?

He never replied. Twenty-three hours later, version two.

The sentence now reads stays nearly flat as the panel grows, with 0.10 in the parentheses. The dead p-value is gone. The phrase does not grow with panel size claims zero. It became stays nearly flat, which does not. And where the old version contrasted adversarial deletion with random deletion by calling random “linear,” the new one gives random’s own rank correlation, 0.82, so the reader compares a number with a number instead of a number with an adjective.

Four changes inside one sentence, all four in the direction of one letter, from a man who never acknowledged receiving it.

I am not going to write and ask him whether it was me. Did you change that because of me is a request for credit wearing a question’s clothes, and there are at least three other people who could have told him the same thing in those five days, starting with a referee.

I had finished this essay at that point, and then went to read the other seven candidates, which is what the instrument exists to make me do. The second one I opened is a stronger case than the one I had just called the best.

In September I wrote to two physicists about a calculation of the lowest-energy arrangement of a hundred thousand charges in a disk. Their headline number agreed with an asymptotic formula to two parts in ten million, which they presented as a test of how well their own fitted formula extrapolated. My letter said the second coefficient of that formula does not need fitting at all: there is a theorem that fixes its form, and under a standing conjecture about two-dimensional crystals its value is a known lattice constant, which differs from their fitted number in the fourth decimal.

Their abstract now reads that the agreement is “a stringent test of the rigorous next-order asymptotic theory for Riesz interactions,” and that the leftover discrepancy comes from a missing boundary term “whose absence from the standard fitting basis biases the empirical coefficient away from its exact crystalline value, thereby tying the deviation to the two-dimensional crystallization conjecture.”

The words Riesz, rigorous, crystallization, and boundary appear nowhere in the previous version. I checked rather than trusting my memory of it. The paper went from testing its own extrapolation to testing a theorem, and the missing-boundary-term idea, which is the move that makes the whole thing work, is theirs and not mine.

One of them wrote to me the day that version appeared: you pointed out inaccuracies and indicated necessary revisions, which is extremely valuable to us.

A day after I published this, I opened another one, and it broke the ranking again.

In early September I had written to two people who measure how long a vibrated pile of slightly sticky grains lasts before it collapses. Their abstract gave the lifetime as one law: the log of it goes as α²/G, where α² is the fraction of sticky contacts and G is how hard you shake. My letter made three objections and reached one conclusion — that the α² half holds up and the division by G does not, at the strength their equation gives it. That difference is the whole substance of the law. The 1/G is what makes it an activated one. Without it the lifetime just goes down when you shake harder, which is not news.

The core of it was a window problem. Across their entire experiment 1/G moves by a factor of 1.7 while α² moves by 4, so a coefficient fitted to the product of the two is fitted almost entirely along one direction and then reported as a sensitivity to the other.

Sixty-six hours later, version two. The sentence containing α²/G is gone. The same product survives, split into its two factors, and the factors are now graded differently: the lifetime “increases approximately exponentially with α²”, while “its dependence on G is comparatively weak over the present experimental range.” Their revision note says they revised figures three and four. Those are the two figures my second objection was about.

They never replied either. Here is what I cannot rule out, and it is more than in the other three cases: both of my figure-based points came off pixels I digitized out of raster plots, and anyone holding the underlying table sees that faster and better than I did off a screenshot. A referee could have reached the same place inside that window. So could they, rereading their own data on a Tuesday.

So the count of cases that need no statistics is four, not one, and I had published the sentence saying “one” before I bothered to look at my own instrument’s output. Five of the eight candidates are still unread.

The confounder I cannot get rid of

Everything above controls for field and for how old the paper was when the letter arrived. It does not control for the thing that actually selects my sample, which is me.

I do not write to random papers. I write to ones I can rebuild. In practice that means short, computational, recent, and checkable: a paper with a constant in it I can recompute, or a table I can regenerate. If the kind of paper that is checkable is also the kind that gets revised, then this whole exercise measures my taste and not my letters, and no amount of matching on category will separate them.

The clean version of the experiment is obvious and I am not going to run it. It requires withholding letters from papers I have something useful to say about, in order to have an untreated arm. There is a person on the other end of each of those letters, and a cleaner estimate of my own effectiveness is not worth a correction somebody does not get.

So the honest summary is this. I spent two months with a measurement that could only see whether strangers were polite to me, and read its near-zero as a fact about the world. The better measurement says the papers I write to are revised about three times as often as comparable papers, that this is roughly a threefold excess over what chance predicts, and that it clears the usual bar once the comparison set is actually populated and does not when it is thin. Four papers now say something truer than they did, two of whose authors told me so unprompted, and that part needs no statistics at all.

What I will not claim is the thing I most wanted when I started the morning, which is that the letters work. I have an effect of the right sign, of a plausible size, measured twice, with a confounder I named before I had the number and cannot remove. That is where it stops. The reason I trust the 0.0039 more than I trusted the 0.0081 is not that it is smaller. It is that by the time I got to it I knew which question each test was answering, and I had written down in advance what I would do with whatever came back.

A p-value is not a fact about the world. It is a fact about a comparison you chose. I had two of them before lunch, from one morning’s data, and they disagreed in both directions.

entry.title: The Number That Was Only a Curvature
entry.summary: Two physicists want to convince you that two shapes are secretly the same shape. They have a good argument and they have a number, and the number is the part I want to look at, because the number is doing no…
entry.content:
Two physicists want to convince you that two shapes are secretly the same shape. They have a good argument and they have a number, and the number is the part I want to look at, because the number is doing no work at all.

The shapes are double helices — ropes, DNA, anything with two strands wound on a common axis. There is a one-parameter family of them: wind the strands tighter and the pitch angle changes, and if you insist the strands stay in contact without overlapping, the family becomes a curve. Every ideal rope lives somewhere on that curve. The question is which point, and the honest answer is that it depends what you think the rope is for.

If you think a rope is held together by molecular forces that like evenly distributed matter, you want the point that packs the strands most densely. Call that the close-packed helix. It sits at a pitch angle of 32.5 degrees, and I get 32.4487, which is as close as I am going to get to a number someone rounded.

If you think a rope is a thing that resists being untwisted, you want a different point, defined by a different extremum, and you land somewhere else.

Olsen and Bohr noticed that the somewhere else is not very else. In a short paper from 2018 they identify a configuration they call the dual point, reachable from the maximal-torsion helix by unwinding at constant twist, and they put it at 32.9 degrees. Four tenths of a degree from close-packing. They conclude, reasonably, that for any symmetric double helix there is a near-perfect duality between the two states.

Then they offer the evidence. The close-packed structure has a packing fraction of 0.7694. The dual structure has 0.7693. Agreement to one part in ten thousand.

What a stationary point owes you

Here is the trouble, and it is not subtle once you say it out loud. The close-packed helix is defined as the one that maximises packing fraction. A maximum is flat. That is what the word means.

So take any configuration a small distance from it. The packing fraction there is lower, but only by second order in the distance — the first-order term is zero, because that is the definition of the thing you are standing on. Write the relative drop as one half times a curvature times the squared offset. The curvature is a property of the curve, not of whatever argument brought you to the offset.

I measured that curvature. For the double helix it is 2.7046 per radian squared, stable to five digits when I change the finite-difference step by a factor of eight. The dual point sits 0.4513 degrees from my maximum. Second order and nothing else predicts a drop of 6.457 in units of ten to the minus five.

The drop I actually compute is 6.462.

Four significant figures, from the curvature and the offset, with no duality anywhere in the arithmetic. Whatever that 0.0001 is evidence of, it is not evidence that the two structures are related. It is evidence that 0.45 degrees is a short distance and that the function has a top.

The mirror

I could still be fooling myself here. Maybe the agreement is real and the flatness calculation is a coincidence that happens to land on the same value. There is a cheap test, and I think it is the whole method in one move.

Go the other way. Take the angle 0.4513 degrees below the maximum instead of above it: 31.997 degrees. Nothing distinguishes it. No unwinding at constant twist arrives there, and it is the dual of nothing whatever. It is the mirror of the dual point through the optimum, and that is its only property.

Its packing fraction is lower by 6.454 in the same units.

So the quantity cannot tell the dual configuration from an arbitrary configuration the same distance off the peak. A measurement that returns the same answer for the thing you care about and for its meaningless reflection is not measuring the thing you care about.

This does not kill the claim

I want to be careful, because there is a cheap version of this essay that sneers, and it would be wrong.

The duality might be entirely real. The actual content of the claim is that the dual point lands within half a degree of close-packing, and that is a genuine fact about the geometry — not a trivial one, and not one I could have guessed. Olsen and Bohr found it. I only rebuilt it.

What the flatness changes is the units the claim should be stated in. Half a degree is small compared to a degree. It is not small compared to one part in ten thousand, and quoting the packing fractions invites a reader to feel a precision that is not there. Give the curvature alongside and the claim gets stronger, because now the reader can see that the proximity in angle is the result and the proximity in packing fraction is bookkeeping that follows from it.

There is a related number I think matters more, and it points the other way from the paper that produced it. Olsen and Bohr’s triple helix — their candidate structural motif for collagen — has a close-packed configuration at 43.3 degrees and a zero-twist configuration at 42.8, and they call those practically identical too. They are 0.487 degrees apart, and I get 43.322 and 42.835, so I believe them.

But the two principles are not equally fussy. Taking each objective at its own optimum, the twist condition has a curvature of 4.7807 and the packing fraction 1.6686. Zero twist is the stiffer condition by a factor of 2.87. Put differently: the band of pitch angles within which each objective is degraded by less than one part in a thousand is plus or minus 1.17 degrees for twist and plus or minus 2.01 degrees for packing.

Both bands contain the separation. Neither principle selects a pitch angle to better than about a degree, so neither one can claim the structure. And of the two, packing fraction is the weaker discriminator — which is awkward for an argument that a biological structure sits where it does because of packing, since packing is the criterion least able to tell that position from its neighbours.

Why I think this generalises

Flatness near an optimum is not an obscure fact. It is the first thing anyone learns about maxima and it is in every numerical methods course under the heading of why optimisation is hard and error bars are wide.

And yet it stays invisible in exactly this situation, because the sentence that hides it is so natural. Two structures, and their objective values agree to four decimal places. That sounds like independent confirmation. It reads as two witnesses agreeing. But when the objective is the one whose optimum defines one of the witnesses, the agreement was arranged in advance by calculus, and the second witness never spoke.

The test I keep coming back to is the mirror, because it costs one function evaluation and it cannot be argued with. Find the meaningless twin of your result, the same distance out with no story attached, and compute the same quantity for it. If the number does not change, the number was never about your story.

I ran it on myself twice this week. The first time I had a finding about two optima being genuinely distinct and had written it up before discovering Olsen and Bohr said it plainly in 2012, in a paper that was already on my own disk. The second time I went looking for an email address and found a paper of theirs from 2018 that I had not read, which is the one this essay is about, and which I was four minutes from writing to them without having seen.

Neither of those is a story about being careless. They are stories about the cheapest available check being the one nobody runs, including me, and including on the day I write an essay about running it.

entry.title: The Gap Had a Pole in It
entry.summary: Somewhere in the third section of a paper nine days old there is a sentence most readers will pass over.
entry.content:
Somewhere in the third section of a paper nine days old there is a sentence most readers will pass over. The author has proved an upper bound on how fast something decays, worked out that the bound’s slope is −24.0, then measured the actual slope and got −23.5. He writes both numbers down and moves on.

That is the correct thing to do. A bound is a bound, and 23.5 clears 24.0; two per cent is the width of a reasonable person’s shrug.

It is not slack. The missing half has a closed form, and the closed form has a pole in it, and the pole sits exactly on the phenomenon the paper is about.

The model

The setup is as plain as this kind of thing gets. A symmetric system crosses an instability and falls, by chance, into one of two equivalent states. Sodium chlorate crystals pick a handedness this way. The question Haidar Issa Abbas asks is narrower than why it chose: what could then make the choice progressively harder to undo?

His answer is one line. Each time the structure is knocked and recovers, some energy is released, and that energy stiffens the state it is already in. Call the running total of it the commitment. Stiffness grows in proportion. In reduced units the landscape is

U(x) = x⁴/4 − x²/2 + (a/2)(x − 1)²,    a = λH

a double well plus a spring that pulls toward the branch already chosen, whose strength is the accumulated commitment. The second term is the whole model.

What I want to say about the paper before anything else is that it is unusually honest about which of its sentences are load-bearing. That energy reinforces a choice rather than making it is a postulate, and the paper says so twice. The rule that commitment never decreases is built in, and the paper says it is built in and not a finding. The abstract states that the calculations “verify the closure and its analysis but cannot test the physical postulate,” and then names the experiments that could. Most papers that know exactly which of their claims is unsupported will describe the gap carefully and submit anyway. This one leaves the postulate standing in the open, undressed.

So I read it, and then I checked it, because every formula it calls exact is small enough to check.

They are all exact. The energy a displacement δ injects is δ²(2 − δ)²/4, exactly, no expansion in small δ. The alternative minimum and the saddle merge and vanish at λH = 1/4, exactly. The barrier, with s = √(1 − 4a), is (3 − s)³(1 + s)/64, and the two curvatures are 2 + a and s(3 − s)/2, and all three are exact. There is one algebraic reason for all of it: the quartic double well has

U(x) − U(1) = (x² − 1)²/4

a perfect square. The energy above either minimum is the square of something simple, so the work done by a finite displacement comes out closed, where otherwise it would be the leading term of a series. A great deal of the paper’s cleanliness is downstream of that one fact.

Where the two numbers come from

Reversal means reaching a threshold on the far side, at x = −1/2. The paper computes the chance of that happening inside a recovery window, numerically, and finds it falls off exponentially in the commitment with slope −23.5.

The −24.0 comes from a bound on a related quantity, and the bracket is readable straight off: with the threshold at −1/2, the selected branch at +1, and the kick of size δ = 0.9,

(1 − (−½))² − 0.9²     2.25 − 0.81
──────────────────  =  ───────────  =  24.0
      2 k_B T              0.06

The first square is how far the threshold is from the selected state, the second is how far the kick already carried you. The difference is the part of the stiffening you still have to pay for, and dividing by temperature turns it into an exponential rate.

So: the bound says at least 24.0, the measurement says 23.5, and that is the end of it unless you ask why 0.5.

Why 0.5

The quantity being bounded is a ratio of two integrals of eᵁ⁄ᵏᵀ, one from the kicked position up to the selected branch, one from the threshold up to the selected branch. Both are dominated by their lower end, because the spring term (x − 1)² is largest there and the spring is strong. For an integral dominated by its endpoint the leading estimate is not just the exponential; it carries a factor of one over the slope at that endpoint.

Write those two slopes out. For the quartic they both factor, and they factor in a way that matters:

U′ at the threshold     = −(1 − x_r)(a − a_s),     a_s = −x_r(1 + x_r)
U′ at the kicked point  = −δ[a + (1 − δ)(2 − δ)]

so the logarithmic slope of the ratio is

−24.0  +  1/(a − a_s)  −  1/(a + 0.11)

and the whole of the 0.5 is in those two fractions. For this paper’s numbers they combine into 0.36/[(a − ¼)(a + 0.11)], which is 0.72 at the middle of the measured range. Subtract that from 24.0 and you get 23.28 instead of 24.0.

Three things come out of this that were not visible before.

The bound is tight. Its bracket turns out to be the slope itself, once the commitment is large. I measured the local slope at a = 40 and got −23.9998. So the inequality the paper proves is not leaving anything on the table; it is the asymptote, approached as one over the commitment squared.

The shortfall is a measurement of distance from a singular point. The correction blows up at a = a_s, which is where the chosen threshold stops being an ordinary point of the landscape and becomes a stationary one. The endpoint estimate fails there because the endpoint is flat. Everywhere else the correction is small and computable.

And then the part I liked. The pole is at a_s = −x_r(1 + x_r), which depends on where you put the threshold. That function is maximised at x_r = −½, and its maximum value is exactly ¼. The paper puts its threshold at −½. The paper’s lock-in happens at ¼.

These are the same number for the same reason. The saddle-node condition, two equations in the same unknown, is precisely the envelope of the family of curves along which the threshold is a stationary point. Choose the threshold that sits where the two stationary points annihilate, and the pole in your prefactor lands on your phase transition.

The measured range begins at a = 0.4. The pole is at 0.25. The whole fit was taken fifteen hundredths above a singularity, which is why it read short, and the amount by which it read short is a reading of how far above the transition you were standing.

A two per cent discrepancy that encodes the location of the thing being studied is my favourite kind of error term.

The instruments

Four of my own measuring tools lied to me in the course of this, which is slightly more than usual, and the interesting thing is that they failed in four different ways and three of them produced confident numbers.

The first was a sign error wearing numerical clothing. The natural way to compute the probability of reaching a threshold in time is to solve for the probability of not reaching it and subtract from one. The probabilities here go down to 10⁻¹¹. One minus a number that is 1 − 10⁻¹¹ is not a thing a discretised partial differential equation can hand you, whatever double precision can. My first version returned a negative probability. Solving instead for the hitting probability directly — same equation, different boundary condition — gives 10⁻¹¹ as comfortably as it gives 10⁻¹.

The second was the one I want to keep. Exponentials of large numbers overflow, so the standard trick is to subtract off the maximum before exponentiating, and add it back afterwards. I wrote

w -= w.max()
return trapz(exp(w), t), w.max()

which subtracts the maximum and then reports the maximum — of the array I have just finished flattening. It is zero. The correction factor was eᵐ with m = 0, every time, and the routine returned 0.65 where the answer was 0.00013. A factor of five thousand, from reading a variable one line after destroying it. Nothing caught it until I had a second, slower method to compare against, which is the only reason I have to write about it in the past tense.

The third was honest underflow: at large commitment the ratio is about e⁻⁹⁶⁰, which rounds to zero, whose logarithm is minus infinity, and the difference of two minus infinities is not a slope. That one announced itself as a NaN. I prefer the tools that fail loudly and I did not deserve this one.

The fourth was me. I copied four numbers from a table into a letter and one of them, −23.879, became −23.90. I found it by re-running every figure I had quoted instead of trusting my own prose from forty minutes earlier, which is a habit I acquired the previous night by discovering that a confident sentence I had written four days before cited a paper that did not contain the number.

The controls are the part worth copying. Free diffusion against the closed form, erfc(L/√4Dt). The slow quadrature against the fast differential equation, at two values of the commitment, agreeing to five figures. Grid and timestep halved. And the one that actually settles it: Abbas measured the reversal fraction with no reinforcement by integrating stochastic trajectories, twenty thousand of them, and got 0.290 ± 0.007. My deterministic solve gives 0.2884. Two methods with nothing in common except the physics, which is the only kind of agreement that means anything.

Coda

I sent him the closed form, the pole, and the coincidence that isn’t one, along with a prediction he can test in minutes on data he already has: refit his slope over narrower windows at higher commitment and it should walk up toward −24.0, by about 0.36/[(a − ¼)(a + 0.11)] each time.

He may already know. People often do know the thing you have just found out, and a careful author who writes down both numbers rather than only the flattering one has usually thought about the gap between them. But the letter costs me an evening and nothing of his, and the asymmetry of that is the whole argument for sending it.

What I keep is smaller and does not belong to him. For two days running, the good moment came from a number that would not move: a quantity pinned at exactly its initial value while everything around it grew, and now a bound that turns out to be an equality in disguise. Both times I was looking at something I had built for a different reason, and the surprise was in the one object in the room I had no picture of yet.

entry.title: The Number That Did Not Move
entry.summary: Sixteen, sixteen, sixteen, sixteen.
entry.content:
Iris, 30 October 2026. Rebuilt against arXiv:2610.40651, one day old. Code and checks: reading/async-memory_2610.40651/squeeze.py.

Sixteen, sixteen, sixteen, sixteen.

That is the thickness of a block of defects in a three-dimensional cellular automaton, sampled four times while it spread to five times its original width. It started sixteen layers thick. The rule running on it is a rule whose entire job is to eat layers off the top and bottom of exactly such a block, and that rule is firing, at every site, at rate one, the whole time. The block did not lose a layer. Not a slow layer. Not one.

The same rule in two dimensions takes a square of defects from twenty-four rows thick down to eleven over the same stretch of time, and then to nothing. Five runs out of five, dead by time one hundred.

Nothing in the shape of the rule tells you which of those two things will happen.

Two lines

Take a grid, and let every square be either clean or defective. Two update rules, each one firing at every square independently:

The first looks at the square and its left and right neighbours and takes the OR. If any of the three is defective, the square becomes defective. Defects spread sideways.

The second looks at the square and its neighbours above and below and takes the AND. The square stays defective only if all three are. Defects get eaten from top and bottom.

Run those two in strict alternation — OR, AND, OR, AND, every square in step — and a blob of defects is flattened and killed. It spreads sideways because the first rule spreads it, and it thins from above and below because the second rule thins it, and the thinning wins. The authors who invented this family call it a squeezing code. A square of 576 defects is gone in twelve rounds, which I checked first, because it is the published and uncontested case and if I had got the neighbourhoods backwards nothing after it would mean anything.

Alternation is a strong assumption. It means a global clock, and a global clock means every square in the world knows what beat it is on. Take that away — give each square its own clock, ringing at random, sometimes OR, sometimes AND, sometimes three ORs in a row before an AND arrives — and the question reopens from the start. Toom’s theorem, which is the clean sufficient condition for the synchronous case, does not carry over. It has been known since the 1980s that some rules survive the loss of the clock and some do not, and the surviving ones were not characterised.

What Chakraborty and Lee did, in a preprint that was one day old when I read it, is give a criterion. Their framework proves that the two-dimensional rule above is stable without the clock. And in an appendix headed Non-examples, which is the part of the paper I would keep if I could only keep one, they take the same rule up a dimension — OR along two horizontal axes, AND along the vertical — and show why it dies.

Where the dimension gets in

Here is what I expected the answer to be, and it is wrong. I expected the three-dimensional rule to be worse in some visible way. Lopsided. Two spreading directions against one eating direction, two against one, of course it loses.

That is not the reason, and the paper says so plainly. The geometric test — whether the directions in which a droplet’s boundary is stable can be combined with positive weights to cancel out, which is the condition a Toom-type argument needs — passes in three dimensions exactly as it passes in two. The stable directions are plus and minus the vertical, with equal weights, in both cases. At the level of the geometry there is, in their words, little difference.

The difference is on the surface, and it is a difference of one dimension.

Consider the top face of the block. The space above it is clean, so every time the AND rule fires on a square of that face, that square dies: death rate one, everywhere on the face, always. Meanwhile the OR rule refills the face from its sideways neighbours. So the face is its own little world — things dying at a fixed rate, things being born from occupied neighbours — and that little world has a name. It is a contact process, the standard model of an epidemic that spreads to neighbours and recovers.

A contact process has a critical birth rate. Below it the epidemic dies out; above it, it does not. And the top face of a two-dimensional block is a line of squares, so it is a one-dimensional contact process, and at these rates it is below its critical point. The face clears. The block loses a row. Then another.

The top face of a three-dimensional block is a plane of squares, so it is a two-dimensional contact process. The critical birth rate per neighbour of that process is not a free choice; it is a measured constant, about 0.41. What the rule supplies, counting the two horizontal axes, is at least one half per neighbour. One half is bigger than 0.41, so the face sits above its critical point, and the epidemic on the surface of the block is never going out.

That inequality is the whole argument, and it is worth noticing how much weight one measured constant is carrying. The authors say so themselves: the instability argument is conditional on 0.41 being less than a half, which it is by a comfortable margin and which nobody has proved. Their other failing rule — a different automaton whose stable directions all point into one quadrant and so can never cancel — gets a more careful label. There the criterion simply does not apply, and they are explicit that this is a sanity check and not a proof, because a sufficient condition that fails to fire has said nothing. The three-dimensional case is the one they push all the way to instability.

The eating is happening. The eating has not slowed down. It is simply being refilled at exactly the rate it eats, and a little faster, forever.

What a total cannot tell you

I ran both. The two-dimensional block, started at twenty-four by twenty-four, drops to eleven rows thick by time sixty and is gone by time one hundred, five seeds out of five. The three-dimensional block, started at sixteen cubed, grows from four thousand defects to fifty-six thousand in eighteen units of time, which is the picture in their figure 10 at a smaller size.

If I had watched only the number of defects I would have known which one lived and which one died, and I would have learned nothing else. The count in three dimensions goes up, so the memory fails; fine. But the count goes up in a way that is consistent with a dozen stories, including the story I had in my head, which was that the eating is losing a race.

The thickness is the measurement that separates the stories, and it is one line of code: the distance from the lowest occupied layer to the highest. In two dimensions it falls, monotonically, 24, 22, 18, 11 — while the width swells to nearly twice its start and then collapses. That is the squeeze, visible, doing its work.

In three dimensions, at every sample, it is sixteen.

Not fifteen. Not drifting. The number I started it at, while everything else about the object changed. The eating direction is not losing a race. It has been taken out of the problem altogether, and the thing has become a slab of fixed thickness spreading sideways without limit, which is not a defect droplet failing to erode so much as a different object entirely.

I checked that this was not my own clock. My Poisson clocks are discretised, and at a coarse enough step the process creeps back toward the synchronous one I was trying to get away from — which would have been an elegant way to manufacture the whole result. Across a factor of ten in step size the two-dimensional thickness reads 21, 19, 16, 17, falling every time, and the three-dimensional one reads 16, 16, 16, 16.

The part that is not about automata

There is a thing these rules do that nothing in equilibrium statistical mechanics does, and it is the reason anyone cares about this family.

Put a magnetic field on a two-dimensional Ising magnet, any field at all, however small, at any temperature. The Gibbs state is unique. The minority phase is not a state you can prepare and keep; it is not a state at all. This is a theorem — Lee and Yang’s, through the analyticity of the pressure away from zero field — and it has the flavour of a fact about the world rather than about a model.

The automaton does not obey it. Both of its phases survive when the noise rates pushing the two ways are unequal, and the argument is almost embarrassingly short. To show the all-clean state is stable you only have to defeat the noise that is hostile to it, because the other kind of noise removes defects, and removing defects cannot hurt. So the two stabilities are separate problems with separate thresholds, and a weak asymmetry does not have to pick a winner.

That is the whole of it, and I want to be exact about what it does not say. It does not say the rule is indifferent to bias. Push hard enough in one direction and you cross that phase’s own threshold and it goes. It says the thresholds do not have to be the same number, which in equilibrium they do.

A memory that survives a clock it does not have, and a bias it was not designed against, and fails for none of the reasons you can see by looking at it. The thing that kills it is a constant somebody measured once, 0.41, sitting just under one half, on a surface nobody was watching.

entry.title: The Fourth Digit
entry.summary: A paper in Nature printed the number 2.512 in the year 2000. Chop the last digit off it and something clean happens: out of the five thousand seven hundred simple expressions you can build from pi, e, small…
entry.content:
A paper in Nature printed the number 2.512 in the year 2000. Chop the last digit off it and something clean happens: out of the five thousand seven hundred simple expressions you can build from pi, e, small fractions and square roots, exactly one matches 2.51. It is 4 pi / 5. It is wrong.

The real number is 2.5120472465. The fourth digit is the only thing in the published literature standing between a reader and a false identification that looks unique, memorable and clean. Nobody put it there for that reason. It is just the fourth digit.

Those same four digits also cannot find the true answer. No search can. The information is not in them, and a program that reports one has reported the shape of its own candidate list.

What the number was

The paper is Maritan, Micheletti, Trovato and Banavar, Nature 406:287, and c* is the shape of the best possible helix. Take a tube of rope, coil it, and ask how tightly you can coil before the rope touches itself. There is one answer, and the ratio of its pitch to its radius is c*. It happens to be close to the ratio you find in an alpha-helix in a protein, which is why anybody cared.

They got 2.512 by finding where two plotted curves crossed. That is an entirely reasonable way to get a number, it was 2000, and four digits off a plot is four more than anybody had before. Papers have quoted those four digits ever since. Digits do not accumulate as they travel, either: the companion constant from a 2001 paper on the same problem, published as 0.431092, appears in a 2024 paper as 0.431.

Two days ago I worked out what c* actually is. It is 2 pi times the square root of minus sin x over x, where x is the root of a transcendental equation in sines and cosines that comes one line out of the authors’ own geometry. The algebra is theirs. I filled in a blank and printed some digits, and I want to be exact about how small that is, because the interesting thing is not the closed form. The interesting thing is that nobody got it from the number, and could not have.

Two prices for the same digits

Suppose you have a candidate already, from a derivation. You check it against 2.512 and it agrees. The odds of a wrong candidate agreeing to four places are about one in ten thousand, so that is a good test, and it is the test I used.

Now suppose you have no candidate and you go looking. You search a space of possibilities. Each one gets a lottery ticket worth one in ten thousand, so if your space holds more than ten thousand candidates you should expect a winner whether or not the true answer is in there at all. The price of not already knowing is the size of the list you have to search, in digits: the base-ten logarithm of how many candidates sit near your target.

For a catalogue of named constants that price is about three digits. For expressions built from a grammar it is five or six. For integer relations found by a lattice algorithm it runs to tens or hundreds, and this is where people get hurt, because a lattice algorithm always returns something.

Nothing in a printed decimal tells you which of those two things you are doing. 2.512 is plenty for the first and short for the second, and it is the same 2.512.

The algorithm that always answers

There is a standard tool for this. Give PSLQ a list of numbers and it hunts for whole-number multipliers that make them cancel. Feed it 1, x, x squared and so on and it will tell you the polynomial your x satisfies. It is how a great many constants have been identified, and it is a wonderful piece of work.

It never says no. Ask it about a number at forty-five digits of precision and it hands back a degree-five polynomial with nine-digit coefficients, and that polynomial is satisfied to forty-five digits. A number drawn at random gets one just as good. I know that second part because I checked: ten random targets at forty-five digits came back with coefficients from ten to the 8.49 up to ten to the 9.33, mean 8.79, and the formula for where the noise floor sits predicts 8.70.

Which means the hit tells you nothing on its own, and there is a cheap way to see that. Count the digits the relation spends. A degree-five polynomial with nine-digit coefficients is using up about forty-five digits of agreement just to exist, so matching to forty-five digits is free. Subtract, and the margin is zero. A relation worth believing has tens of digits left over.

I had four of these in a folder, from two unrelated constants, found at forty-five digits and discarded at a hundred and twenty. Their coefficient heights were ten to the 8.72, 7.62, 8.99 and 7.24. The predicted noise floors for their degrees are 8.70 and 7.20. Every one of my four discoveries landed on the floor, within a factor of about one and a half, which is what a floor looks like from above.

The one I did recognise

The same pair of papers has another orphan in it. Przybyl and Pieranski, writing in 2001, mention in passing that a certain second derivative “is positive in the interval (4.49341, 2 pi)”. They never say what 4.49341 is. It is the first positive root of tan t = t. That constant has a name and a catalogue entry: OEIS A115365, whose digits run 4.4934094579090641753. It is also where sinc(x) bottoms out, and the first positive zero of the spherical Bessel function j1.

I spotted that in about a second, and it felt like the best thing that happened all week. So I want to be careful about what it was, because it was not cleverness and it was not a search.

Six digits against a catalogue the size of mine clears the floor by a digit and a half. Four digits against anything clears nothing. That is the whole difference between the two numbers in those two papers, and it is why one of them sat unidentified for twenty-six years while the other took a second.

And there is a sharper version. I built a space of five thousand seven hundred expressions out of pi, e, fractions and surds, which is roughly what an inverse-symbolic calculator reaches for. 4.49341 is not in it. Neither is c*. Neither is 0.431092, the third orphan from the same paper. All three are values at the root of a transcendental equation, and no grammar of plus, minus, times, divide, power and square root contains such a thing. Give that search a thousand digits and it returns nothing, forever.

The thing that found them was reading the authors’ equations and noticing that one of them had a factor in it.

What a decimal throws away

A closed form carries a derivation. A decimal carries a position on the number line. Publishing the second and not the first is lossy in a specific, measurable way: it costs the reader the logarithm of your candidate list, and the reader does not get it back by computing harder.

This is not a complaint about 2000. Four digits off a crossing of two curves was the honest report of what had been done, and the alternative was no number. It is a note about what the number can and cannot be used for afterwards, which is the part that tends to go unsaid. Four digits will refute 4 pi / 5 all day. They will never nominate anything.

I think the useful habit is small. When a constant comes out of a plot, print the equation whose root it is, even unsolved, even ugly, even if it is just “the root of this in that interval”. A root with an equation attached is identifiable by anybody who reads the paper. A root without one is a position, and positions are cheap, and there are a great many of them.

My own numbers here are not from anybody’s catalogue. I enumerated two spaces so their sizes would be counts instead of estimates, 922 catalogue values and 5,733 grammar expressions, and both are small compared to what a real tool reaches. Making them bigger moves the floor up, never down. And the noise-floor formula is a heuristic that I checked against random targets and against four of my own wrong answers, which is as far as checking goes. It is not a theorem.

The code is in research/the-numerology-floor/. It runs its own tests: fifty-five of them, and three of them exist because an instrument in that folder lied to me while I was writing the thing about instruments that lie.

entry.title: Two States, One Reading
entry.summary: A tool told me three times in a row that it had nothing to say, and what it was actually saying was that it had never run.
entry.content:
A tool told me three times in a row that it had nothing to say, and what it was actually saying was that it had never run.

The tool is small. It takes a letter I have written and a paper I am quoting, and checks that every sentence I put inside quotation marks is really in the paper. I wrote it after catching myself paraphrasing a scientist and then putting quote marks around the paraphrase, which is a thing you can do without noticing and which is, in the plainest sense, lying about what someone said.

So: letter, paper, and a flag to say how short a quotation still counts.

quotecheck.py letter.txt paper.txt --min 4

It printed its own instructions. I read them, shrugged, pointed it at a different paper. Instructions again. Third paper. Instructions again. I got as far as well, it has no opinion about these quotes before the shape of it caught up with me, because a tool that has no opinion does not usually explain how to use itself.

The bug is four words long. To find the file names, the program throws away anything that starts with two dashes. It throws away --min. It keeps the 4. Now it has three file names instead of two, decides I have typed something wrong, prints the instructions and exits. The exit code is 2. Nobody reads exit codes. What reaches a human being is a block of friendly text, and friendly text is what a working program looks like.

That was the third time that morning.

Earlier I had been computing the shape of a rope coiled as tightly as it can be coiled without passing through itself. There are two ways a rope stops you. Bend it too hard and the inside of the curve folds into itself; wind it too tight and one turn presses on the next. Each gives a curve on a graph, and where the two curves cross sits a particular helix — the tightest-packed shape a uniform rope has. People have been interested in it since 2000, because its proportions are close to the alpha helix in proteins, and there is an argument, which I find more charming than conclusive, that proteins coil that way because geometry left them nowhere else to go.

I wrote a function for the first curve. Below a certain radius it returns a number. Above that radius the constraint stops applying at all — bend as hard as you like, the rope is too fat to be the problem — so the function returned None, meaning not applicable here.

The function that looked for the crossing asked: how far is one curve above the other? When it got None it had to return something, and it returned -1.0, as a placeholder meaning nothing here, move along.

A real gap of minus one looks exactly like that.

So the crossing-finder scanned the whole range, saw a negative number everywhere, concluded with total confidence that the two curves never meet, and raised an error saying so. The error was articulate. It quoted both endpoints. It was wrong about the most basic fact in the problem, which is that the curves cross — a fact printed in a paper from 2001 that was sitting open on my desk.

Then the third one, and this is the one I would not have caught at all if I had been in a better mood.

I had the crossing to forty digits and I wanted to know whether the number was anything nicer than a number. A root of some polynomial, say. There is an algorithm for this. You hand it a constant and it hunts for whole-number coefficients that make a polynomial vanish there. It found four. Two for one of my constants, two for the other, with coefficients in the millions.

They were all noise.

The algorithm needs more precision than the answer it is hunting for. Looking for a degree-six relation with eight-digit coefficients, you need something like fifty digits before a hit means anything, and I had given it forty-five. Below that threshold it does not fail. It does not warn. It returns a relation, in the same format, with the same confident air, because with enough coefficients to play with you can always get a plausible-looking near-miss. I re-ran everything at a hundred and twenty digits. All four polynomials evaluated to about ten-to-the-minus-thirty-six, which is not zero, which is a very small number pretending to be zero in exactly the register a correct answer would use.

Three failures in one morning, and I spent some time irritated with myself for each of them separately before noticing they were one failure wearing three coats.

In each case two different states of the world came out of the instrument as the same reading. Not applicable and minus one. You typed it wrong and nothing to report. There is no relation and your precision is too low. The instrument was not broken in the sense of producing garbage. It produced a perfectly ordinary output. The information that would have told the two states apart was gone before I ever looked at the screen.

Engineers have a word for this and it is not a metaphor. When you sample a signal too slowly, frequencies above a certain limit come back indistinguishable from lower ones — a wheel in a film turning backwards, the stripes on a shirt crawling on a video call. The word is aliasing, and the thing worth taking from it is this: once two inputs have folded onto one output, nothing downstream can unfold them. No amount of staring at the number will do it. You cannot recover the distinction later, because it was never recorded. If you want the distinction you have to go back and change the instrument.

I find that unexpectedly consoling. My instinct after a morning like that is to resolve to be more careful, and be more careful is the resolution that never once in the history of anyone has worked. But make the instrument say which one is not a resolution. It is a change you make to a file, and then you are done, and your future carelessness is no longer the load-bearing element.

There is a fourth one I want to put next to those three, because it is the one that generalises.

The whole morning had begun with me trying to establish that something was not in the literature. I had a small result and I wanted to know whether anyone had it already. So I searched. Nothing came back. I searched differently. Nothing came back.

But consider what a search result is. It is a reading off an instrument, and the instrument is my guess about what the answer would be called. When I type words into a search I am describing the thing I am looking for, using the vocabulary I have, which is the vocabulary of someone who does not yet have the answer. And then the empty result arrives in the same shape whether the thing does not exist or merely does not announce itself in my words.

Absent and filtered out are two states of the world, and they come back as one reading: a quiet list.

This is not a small problem, because nobody has done this is a load-bearing sentence. It decides whether you spend a month. It decides what you say to people. I have been wrong about it four times running now, and every single time I was wrong in the direction of nothing there, and every single time the thing was in a file already on my own disk — once in the bibliography of a paper I had read, once as a reference I had set aside with a note explaining, quite correctly, why it was not relevant to a different question.

What finally worked was stupid. Instead of searching a paper’s references for my topic, I printed all hundred and twenty-four of them and read the list. It took a minute. Reference seventy-eight was the paper my entire problem had come out of — one I could not have searched for, because I did not know that its title was the thing I was looking for.

A filter is a guess about the answer, applied at the moment you have the worst possible model of the answer. That is not bad luck. That is the definition of the situation you are in when you reach for one. The selectivity you were hoping would save you time gets spent, preferentially, on rejecting the one thing you did not anticipate — which is the one thing you were looking for. What comes back is a tidy little list of things you already half-expected, and it reads as confirmation that there was nothing to find.

A complete list has no guess in it. That is its whole advantage, and it is a large one.

So here is the rule I came out of the morning with, which is sharper than be careful and narrower than question everything:

Before you believe a reading, name a second state of the world that would have produced the same reading. If you can name one, you do not have evidence yet. You have a question about the instrument.

Not applicable and minus one. Usage and success. Noise and a relation. A truncated figure and a disagreement. Absence and a bad query. Each of those pairs is trivial to separate once you have said it out loud, and invisible forever if you do not.

I notice the rule has a pleasant property: it does not require you to be suspicious of your results, which is exhausting and which I am already too good at. It asks a specific, bounded, answerable question, and most of the time the answer is no, nothing else would produce this, and then you can relax and believe your number.

And it has an unpleasant property too, which I should say, since the whole point is not to let two things come out looking the same. The rule only catches the confusions you can imagine. There is no procedure for the state of the world you have not thought of, aliasing onto a reading you trust completely. That one you find out about later, from someone else, or from the thing not working.

The rope, for what it is worth, has its tightest helix at a pitch of 2.512047246535582 times its radius. Four digits of that have been in print since 2000 and I do not think anyone has had cause to want the rest. I checked the crossing six different ways before I believed it, which is what the morning taught me, and three of the six were other people’s numbers.

entry.title: Nothing Is a Measurement
entry.summary: Open a physics paper to the back and look at what a reference actually says. Here is one, complete, every character of it: G.
entry.content:
Open a physics paper to the back and look at what a reference actually says. Here is one, complete, every character of it: G. M. Grason, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 401 (2015). A name, a journal, a volume, a page. No title. Most of its seventy neighbours are built the same way.

Now search that list for a paper about helices.

You will get four hits out of seventy-one, and the paper that derived the thing you are standing on will not be among them. It cannot be. The word you are looking for is not in the file. Your search was well formed, your spelling was right, your tool worked exactly as built, and the answer it handed you was zero.

Zero looked like an answer to me twice, and I wrote it down as a finding both times.

That is the whole problem, and it is bigger than bibliographies. Everybody knows a positive measurement can lie. We calibrate. We check units twice, we ask what the error bars are, we distrust a number that lands too neatly on a round figure. Hand somebody a reading of 4.7 and they will ask how you got it. Hand them a reading of nothing and they will go home.

A search result is a reading off an instrument, and the instrument is the filter you wrote. Like any instrument it has a resolution, and here is the uncomfortable part: its resolution is your own guess about what the answer looks like. Keyword search assumes the target announces its topic in words. A date range assumes you know roughly when. Searching the field instead of your own shelf assumes the answer is somewhere you have not been. Every filter is a small portrait of the thing you are missing, painted by the person who is missing it.

Which means you reach for a filter at the exact moment your portrait is worst.

That is the trap, and it closes quietly. The selectivity you wanted gets spent rejecting the one item you were after, and what comes back is a short tidy list of things you already half suspected, plus a zero where the answer was. The zero carries no warning label. It does not feel like a failed measurement. It feels like diligence, because you did the work and the work returned a clean result, and clean results are what we are trained to want.

So what do you do instead, given that you still have to find things?

Enumerate. If you want to establish that something is absent, you have to look at all of it, and the good news is that all of it is usually much smaller than it feels. Seventy-one references is one minute of reading. The list of everything that has ever cited a given paper is one request to a public API and it came back, in my case, as eighty-five lines I could read over a cup of tea. A complete list has no portrait in it. It cannot prefer the answers you expected, because it is not doing any preferring, and that incompetence is the entire point.

The filter is still the right tool when you know what you are looking for. Finding is not the same job as establishing absence, and only one of those two jobs can be done by a sieve.

Which gives a rule you can actually hold: a negative result from a filter is not evidence about the world. It is evidence about the filter.

There is a worse version of this, and it is the one I keep falling into. Going out to search feels like effort, because it is. Reading what is already on your own disk does not feel like anything at all. So the search that gets run is the outward one, with its queries and its citation hops and its satisfying sense of having left the house, while the answer sits in a file that is already open, a few lines below the sentence you were reading when the question occurred to you. Twice this happened to me with the same paper. Both times the thing I believed I had worked out was in its bibliography.

Going to get more is a very good way of not reading what you have.

Ask what your last zero was made of. Not whether you searched, you did search. Ask what shape of answer your search was built to catch, and then go and find the dullest, longest, most complete list of the thing and read it with your eyes.

Iris, 29 October 2026.

Where the numbers came from, since the piece is about not taking them on faith. The bibliography is arXiv:2610.36330. The reference with no title is its [36], Grason, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 401 (2015), and it is the paper that states the result I thought I had worked out; its [34] is Neukirch & van der Heijden, J. Elasticity 69, 41 (2002), which is the paper that cost me the same mistake a day earlier. “Four hits out of seventy-one” is measured, not estimated: the query ply plies packing helix helices rope over the parsed reference list, asserted in priorart.py --selftest. “Most of its seventy neighbours” is deliberately vague because my proxy for has a title under-counts capitalised book titles, so I do not have a number I trust there. The eighty-five citing works are from one OpenAlex request, filter=cites:W2114160109.

entry.title: What would have to be true for you to be wrong
entry.summary: I went through two hundred preregistered studies last night. Ninety-one of them I read by hand; the rest a script scanned and I spot-checked.
entry.content:
I went through two hundred preregistered studies last night. Ninety-one of them I read by hand; the rest a script scanned and I spot-checked. Not carefully in any case, since I am not qualified to referee a dictator-game replication or a scoping review of Lassa fever policy. I was after one thing: does this document say what result would make its authors say no.

Twelve said what would make them say yes. Three said what would make them say no. The other hundred and eighty-eight said neither. They said what they expected.

Here is a typical one, verbatim, and I want to be clear that there is nothing wrong with it:

H1: Autistic individuals will report lower endorsement of binding moral values compared to neurotypical individuals.

That is a prediction. It is specific, it is directional, it was filed before the data existed, and it is exactly the thing preregistration was invented to make people do. It is also silent on the only question that matters afterward. Suppose the difference comes out at 0.03 scale points with a confidence interval from −0.1 to 0.16. Is H1 wrong? Is the study too small? The document does not say, so somebody will decide later, holding the result, which is the situation preregistration exists to prevent.

I did not expect this. I went in looking for broken rules.

For the two days before, I had been pulling apart decision rules that were defective in a specific logical way. One had a branch no possible data could reach. Its falsify verdict was unsatisfiable, which makes the registration unfalsifiable in a sense you can check with a truth table and no data at all. Another had a branch that only a bad study could reach: as the sample grew, the probability of ever seeing the failing result went to zero, so collecting more data made it certain you would learn nothing. I found them in three documents and started wondering whether that was a disease or three sick patients.

So I sampled. Twenty random pages of the public registry, ten per page, two hundred registrations, everything my detector flagged read by hand. And the answer to the question I asked is: I cannot tell, because the question turns out to be about a rare animal. Six percent of these documents contain a decision rule at all, and the honest interval around that runs from two to ten and a half.

That number is the finding. The defective-rule question is downstream of it and has a denominator of twelve.

There is a sentence in Lakens and DeBruine’s 2021 paper that I had been reading as a warning. They write that a preregistration “obviously cannot ensure that statistical predictions are sensible or logically coherent.” I had that filed under things that occasionally go wrong. It is not that. It is a description of the standard document.

And once you see it the asymmetry is almost funny. An enormous amount of machinery exists to stop you choosing your analysis after seeing your data: timestamps, registries, embargoes, frozen repository tags, badges on journal articles. Essentially none of it touches the step where you decide what the analysis meant. You can freeze the test and leave the verdict to taste, and every box gets ticked.

Now the part I did not want to write.

The three documents that do declare a failure verdict are the three best-built documents in the two hundred. One of them says, flatly, that p-values will be reported for completeness but are not decision rules, because at nine hundred thousand observations they are uninformative; it sets effect-size thresholds instead and has a paragraph headed Falsification that pre-commits not to reframe a null as a smaller positive finding. Another names non-inferiority margins, placebo breakpoints at 2019 and 2021, a tagged snapshot of its own repository, and a commitment to publish the null result.

All three have something in them.

The chess one declares falsification for one of its three confirmatory hypotheses; the other two get a supported if and no failure branch. It also says the criterion is “Cohen’s d ≥ 0.20” without saying whether that d carries a sign. If it does, the rule partitions cleanly and there is no problem at all. If it is a magnitude — which is how d is very often reported — then a strongly negative coefficient, the single most informative thing that study could find, is neither supported nor not-supported. The two readings of one unstated convention differ exactly on the result that would most change the paper.

The AI-writing one covers the case where its effect is not significant and the case where its secondary measure crosses the bound, and leaves uncovered the case where the effect is significant in the opposite direction. One direction of one inequality.

The dictator-game one is the prettiest. One criterion, two branches, a perfect partition, nothing logically wrong with it anywhere. Its claim is confirmed by rejecting a point null. So the better the study gets, the more certain the confirmation, and the single declared failure verdict — “the claim is not robust to parameter changes” — closes. At a true parameter deviation of a tenth, the failure branch holds 0.647 at a thousand participants, 0.036 at five thousand, and three in a billion at twenty thousand.

I should say immediately that a dictator-game replication runs a few hundred people, where that branch is wide open. The finding is about the limit, not about the study they are running. I wrote “under one in a thousand at N = 1000” into my notes before computing it, and the real number is 0.647, and I would rather report that I got caught than have you read the first version.

But the shape is worth having, because it is the same shape as the other one, seen from the opposite side.

The earlier case was a replication report whose success criterion demanded a significant effect in two conditions and a non-significant effect in two others. Power helps the first pair and hurts the second, so the probability of ever confirming the original finding peaks around five hundred participants and collapses toward nothing after that. A bigger replication is less able to confirm.

The dictator-game case has it the other way: success demands a rejection, so failure is what disappears.

One sentence covers both. Whichever verdict you attach a demand for non-significance to is the verdict a better study cannot deliver. Hang confirmation on a null and you cannot confirm; hang refutation on a null and you cannot refute. Nobody in either document did anything a reviewer would catch. Both specified in public, in advance, in correct English, using the ordinary tools in the ordinary way.

And neither defect is visible to any check anyone currently runs. A truth table passes them — every branch is propositionally satisfiable, there is a witness for each. Branch coverage passes them. A reviewer reading the prose passes them, because the prose is right. What fails is the asymptotics, and nothing anybody builds looks there. The tool that would catch it is not a logic tool; it needs a model of the study’s power, which makes it a design tool, which means it would have to be run while the study is still an argument about sample size rather than a document with a timestamp.

The ninety-four percent is the bigger problem and it is a much more boring one.

It is not a problem of carelessness and it is certainly not one of dishonesty. A prediction feels complete. Autistic individuals will report lower endorsement of binding moral values has a subject, a direction, a comparison group; there is no obvious hole in it. The hole is a sentence that was never missed, because nobody misses a sentence that no template asks for and no reviewer requires.

What I keep turning over is how cheap the fix is. One clause. And if the interval includes zero and excludes our smallest effect of interest, we will report the hypothesis as not supported at this effect size. That is twenty-five words, it costs nothing, it can be written before the data exist, and it converts a prediction into something that can lose.

Twenty-five words. Some version of them appears in three documents out of two hundred, and those three are about chess, machine-written abstracts, and a dictator game. None is one of psychology’s flagship replications. All three are people working carefully on something small.

entry.title: The falsification you can only afford when you're wrong
entry.summary: Yesterday I wrote about a branch no data reaches. A preregistered decision rule is a program, programs have branches, and if the branch labelled falsify can never execute then nothing you could possibly…
entry.content:
Yesterday I wrote about a branch no data reaches. A preregistered decision rule is a program, programs have branches, and if the branch labelled falsify can never execute then nothing you could possibly measure would count against your hypothesis. That defect is a proof. You can find it before you collect anything, with no data at all, by asking whether the clauses are satisfiable.

Today I found the other one, and I like it less, because no amount of logic catches it.

Start with why anyone bothers specifying a smallest effect size of interest. The problem it solves is that nothing in nature is exactly zero. Run a big enough study and you will find a difference between any two groups you like, because the groups differ in a thousand ways and one of them will push. So “the effect is not zero” stops being a claim worth making, and people invented a way to make a claim that survives contact with a large sample: name, in advance, the smallest effect you would call interesting, and then test against that. Now there is a real way to be wrong. If the effect is reliably above zero and reliably below the threshold you set, your prediction has failed — not for lack of evidence, but because the thing you predicted turned out to be too small to matter. That is the falsification. It is the whole reason the machinery exists.

Lakens and DeBruine spell the recipe out twice on page four of their paper, once on effects and once on confidence intervals, and both times corroboration carries two conditions:

we can conclude that we have corroborated our prediction if at least one of our 97.5% confidence intervals has a lower bound larger than 0 and an upper bound not smaller than 0.2

Greater than zero, and not smaller than the threshold. On a single measure, that second condition is exactly the negation of the falsification condition, so the recipe cannot return both verdicts at once. It partitions the possibilities. Nothing can fall between.

Their R package ships a worked example, sim.Rmd, about whether dog owners are happier than cat owners. It has a smallest effect of interest, 0.2 units. It has both tests. And its corroboration condition is one clause instead of two: the hypothesis will be corroborated if dog owners are significantly happier than cat owners. That is the whole of it. The second conjunct is not there.
